module_introduction.text:
Hello! This module is about Subject-Verb Agreement. This sounds technical, but it's a simple idea: the subject (who or what is doing the action) must match the verb (the action). If the subject is singular (one person, like 'Ngono'), the verb must be singular. If the subject is plural (many, like 'students'), the verb must be plural.

Why is this challenging? Because of one small letter: 's'. In French, an 's' on a noun makes it plural ("les étudiants"). In English, an 's' on a present tense verb makes it singular ("he speaks"). This is opposite! Also, French uses "il y a" for both singular and plural, but English changes between "There is" and "There are". We will practice this until it becomes automatic.

contrastive_explanation.text:
Let's look at the main differences that cause mistakes.

The Third Person '-s' (The BIGGEST problem):

In English, the Present Simple verb only changes for the third person singular (He, She, It). We add an '-s'.

I speak, You speak, He/She/It speaks, We speak, They speak.

French Connection: In French, verbs are conjugated for all subjects ("je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons..."). Because you don't add an 's' for "je" or "tu", it's easy to forget it for "he" or "she".

The '-s' trap: In French, '-s' on a noun means plural ("les amis"). In English, '-s' on a verb means singular ("my friend speaks"). This is very confusing.

Tip: Remember this rule: "He, She, It = Verb + s".

There is / There are:

In French, you always use "Il y a".

Example: "Il y a un problème." (Singular) / "Il y a des problèmes." (Plural). The verb ("y a") does not change.

In English, you must change the verb to agree with the noun that follows it.

Example: "There is a problem." (Singular) / "There are problems." (Plural)

Tip: If the noun is plural (ends in 's' or is an irregular plural like 'people'), use There are.

Compound Subjects (and / or):

When you connect two subjects with 'and', the subject becomes plural. This is usually the same in French.

Example: "Muna and Foncha are friends." ("Muna et Foncha sont amis.")

The Interrupter Trap: The mistake happens when a phrase comes between the subject and the verb.

Example: "The box of mangoes is heavy." The subject is 'box' (singular), not 'mangoes' (plural). You must agree with 'box'. This is similar in French ("La boîte de mangues est lourde"), but the long English phrase can be distracting.

Collective Nouns:

These are words for groups (family, team, government, class).

In English, these are usually treated as singular (one unit).

Example: "My family lives in Yaoundé." (The family unit).

The "People" Exception: The word 'people' is always plural in English! This is a major error.

French Connection: "Les gens sont..." (plural). Just remember: People = They. People are.

common_errors.wrong: My sister speak English very well.
common_errors.correct: My sister speaks English very well.
common_errors.french_connection: "Ma sœur parle..." The verb 'parle' has no 's' sound. Students forget to add the third-person '-s' for 'she'.

common_errors.wrong: He live in a small house in the quartier.
common_errors.correct: He lives in a small house in the quartier.
common_errors.french_connection: "Il habite..." (no 's'). This is the most common S-V agreement error.
"Il pleut." The verb 'pleut' is third-person, but students forget the English '-s' rule for 'it'.

common_errors.wrong: The new teacher don't give much homework.
common_errors.correct: The new teacher doesn't give much homework.
common_errors.french_connection: 'Don't' = do not. 'Doesn't' = does not. For 'he' or 'she' (the teacher), the auxiliary verb must be 'does'.

common_errors.wrong: My parents works in the same office.
common_errors.correct: My parents work in the same office.
common_errors.french_connection: Students learn the '-s' rule and then over-use it. 'Parents' is plural ('they'), so the verb does not take an '-s'.
"Les étudiants marchent..." The plural verb in French is silent. Students add an 's' because 'students' is plural, but this is the opposite of the English rule.

common_errors.wrong: There is two big mango trees in our compound.
common_errors.correct: There are two big mango trees in our compound.
common_errors.french_connection: French uses "Il y a..." for everything. English must use "There are" for plural nouns ("two trees").

common_errors.wrong: There is many people at the motor park.
common_errors.correct: There are many people at the motor park.
common_errors.french_connection: "Il y a beaucoup de gens..." Again, "Il y a" causes the error. Also, 'people' is plural, so it must be "are".
"Y a-t-il des problèmes ?" The French verb is singular "a". English must use the plural 'are' to match 'problems'.

common_errors.wrong: People is friendly in my village.
common_errors.correct: People are friendly in my village.
common_errors.french_connection: 'People' is always plural. It's like 'they'. (They are friendly). French "Les gens sont..." is also plural, but this is a very common mistake.
When speaking about the family as one unit, we use a singular verb. This is the same in French ('Ma famille est grande').

common_errors.wrong: Foncha and Njoya is playing football.
common_errors.correct: Foncha and Njoya are playing football.
common_errors.french_connection: 'Foncha and Njoya' = 'They' (plural). "Ils sont..." This is a compound subject, so the verb must be plural.

common_errors.wrong: One of my friends live in Bamenda.
common_errors.correct: One of my friends lives in Bamenda.
common_errors.french_connection: The subject is 'One' (singular), not 'friends' (plural). "Un de mes amis habite..." (singular verb). The phrase 'of my friends' is a distraction.

common_errors.wrong: The quality of the plantains are not good.
common_errors.correct: The quality of the plantains is not good.
common_errors.french_connection: The subject is 'quality' (singular), not 'plantains' (plural). "La qualité... est..." The verb agrees with 'quality'.

common_errors.wrong: The president, with his bodyguards, are here.
common_errors.correct: The president, with his bodyguards, is here.
common_errors.french_connection: The main subject is 'The president' (singular). The phrase 'with his bodyguards' is an interrupter. The verb agrees with the main subject.

common_errors.wrong: The children in my class needs help with reading.
common_errors.correct: The children in my class need help with reading.
common_errors.french_connection: The subject is 'The children' (plural), not 'my class' (singular). "Les enfants... ont besoin..." The phrase 'in my class' is an interrupter. Don't let it confuse you!

form_a_questions.question_text: My uncle ___ in Yaoundé.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! The subject is 'My uncle' (he). For He, She, or It in the present simple, we must add '-s' to the verb.

form_a_questions.question_text: Our teacher, Mr. Atangana, ___ very fast.
form_a_questions.feedback: That's right. The subject is 'Our teacher' (he). Remember the rule: He, She, It = Verb + s.

form_a_questions.question_text: Ngono ___ like couscous.
form_a_questions.feedback: Excellent! For negatives with 'he', 'she', or 'it', we must use doesn't (does not), not 'don't' (do not).

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "My phone not work."
form_a_questions.feedback: You found it! The subject 'My phone' is 'it'. The correct negative form for 'it' in the present simple is 'doesn't work'.

form_a_questions.question_text: The students ___ their uniforms to school.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! The subject 'The students' is plural ('they'). We only add '-s' to the verb for singular subjects (he, she, it).

form_a_questions.question_text: We often ___ our grandparents in the village.
form_a_questions.feedback: Good job. The subject is 'We'. The verb only takes an '-s' for 'he', 'she', or 'it'. For 'I', 'you', 'we', and 'they', we use the base verb ('visit').

form_a_questions.question_text: My brothers ___ football in the compound.
form_a_questions.feedback: That's right. 'My brothers' is a plural subject ('they'). The verb 'play' does not need an '-s'.

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "These mangoes tastes very sweet."
form_a_questions.feedback: You spotted the error! The subject is 'These mangoes', which is plural ('they'). We must remove the '-s' from the verb.

form_a_questions.question_text: ___ a lot of bendskins (moto-taxis) in Douala.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! In French, you say "Il y a", but in English, we look at the noun. 'Bendskins' is plural, so we must use "There are".

form_a_questions.question_text: Excuse me, ___ a good pharmacy near here?
form_a_questions.feedback: That's it. We are asking about "a good pharmacy" (singular), so we use "Is there...".

form_a_questions.question_text: ___ any chalk in the classroom?
form_a_questions.feedback: Good! 'Chalk' is an uncountable noun, and uncountable nouns are always treated as singular. So, we use "Is there". (Other uncountable nouns: water, money, rice, sugar.)

form_a_questions.question_text: Look! ___ two men fighting.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! 'Two men' is plural. We use "There are" for plural nouns. Remember: French uses "Il y a" for both singular and plural, but English must change.

form_a_questions.question_text: Many people in Cameroon ___ more than one language.
form_a_questions.feedback: Perfect! 'People' is always plural in English (like 'they'). We must use the plural verb 'speak', not 'speaks'. This is a very common mistake.

form_a_questions.question_text: The national team ___ won many matches this year.
form_a_questions.feedback: Well done! 'Team' is a collective noun. When we talk about the team as one unit, we use a singular verb ('has').

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "People in my neighborhood is very kind."
form_a_questions.feedback: You got it! 'People' is always plural, so we must use 'are', not 'is'. People = They.

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "The class are starting now."
form_a_questions.feedback: Excellent! When we talk about 'the class' as one unit (not individual students), we use a singular verb. The correct sentence is "The class is starting now."

form_a_questions.question_text: My brother and my sister ___ in the same school.
form_a_questions.feedback: That's right! When two subjects are connected with 'and', the subject becomes plural. 'My brother and my sister' = 'They'. So we use the plural verb 'study'.

form_a_questions.question_text: One of the boys in my class ___ from Bamenda.
form_a_questions.feedback: Perfect! The subject is 'One' (singular), not 'the boys' (plural). The phrase 'of the boys in my class' is an interrupter. We must use the singular verb 'comes'.

form_a_questions.question_text: The price of mangoes ___ very high this season.
form_a_questions.feedback: Excellent! The subject is 'The price' (singular), not 'mangoes' (plural). The phrase 'of mangoes' is an interrupter. The verb must agree with 'price', so we use 'is'.

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "The minister, along with his advisors, are coming."
form_a_questions.feedback: You found it! The main subject is 'The minister' (singular). The phrase 'along with his advisors' is extra information. The verb must agree with 'The minister', so we use 'is', not 'are'.

form_b_questions.question_text: My aunt ___ at a hospital in Douala.
form_b_questions.feedback: Correct! The subject is 'My aunt' (she). For He, She, or It in the present simple, we must add '-s' to the verb.

form_b_questions.question_text: The principal of our school, Madame Ekane, ___ three languages.
form_b_questions.feedback: That's right! The subject is 'The principal' (she). Remember the rule: He, She, It = Verb + s.

form_b_questions.question_text: My brother ___ watch CRTV often.
form_b_questions.feedback: Excellent! For negatives with 'he', 'she', or 'it', we must use doesn't (does not), not 'don't' (do not).

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "This kaba (dress) look very beautiful."
form_b_questions.feedback: You found it! The subject 'This kaba' is 'it'. The verb must have an '-s' for third person singular: "looks".

form_b_questions.question_text: The shops in my neighborhood ___ late.
form_b_questions.feedback: Correct! The subject 'The shops' is plural ('they'). We only add '-s' to the verb for singular subjects (he, she, it).

form_b_questions.question_text: We ___ to the radio every morning.
form_b_questions.feedback: Good job! The subject is 'We'. The verb only takes an '-s' for 'he', 'she', or 'it'. For 'we', we use the base verb ('listen').

form_b_questions.question_text: They ___ many cousins in their village.
form_b_questions.feedback: That's right! 'They' is a plural subject. The verb 'have' does not need an '-s'. (Only 'he', 'she', 'it' would use 'has'.)

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "My friends visits me often."
form_b_questions.feedback: You spotted the error! The subject is 'My friends', which is plural ('they'). We must remove the '-s' from the verb: "visit".

form_b_questions.question_text: ___ many different quartiers in Yaoundé.
form_b_questions.feedback: Correct! In French, you say "Il y a", but in English, we look at the noun. 'Quartiers' is plural, so we must use "There are".

form_b_questions.question_text: Look, ___ a message for you on WhatsApp.
form_b_questions.feedback: That's it! We are talking about "a message" (singular), so we use "There is...".

form_b_questions.question_text: ___ any mobile money in your account?
form_b_questions.feedback: Good! 'Mobile money' is an uncountable noun, and uncountable nouns are always treated as singular. So, we use "Is there".

form_b_questions.question_text: ___ five children in their family.
form_b_questions.feedback: Correct! 'Five children' is plural. We use "There are" for plural nouns. Remember: French uses "Il y a" for both, but English must change.

form_b_questions.question_text: Many people in our quartier ___ French and English.
form_b_questions.feedback: Perfect! 'People' is always plural in English (like 'they'). We must use the plural verb 'speak', not 'speaks'.

form_b_questions.question_text: The government ___ announced a new holiday.
form_b_questions.feedback: Well done! 'Government' is a collective noun. When we talk about the government as one unit, we use a singular verb ('has').

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "The police in Douala is very active."
form_b_questions.feedback: You got it! 'Police' is always plural in English, so we must use 'are', not 'is'. Police = They.

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "The committee are deciding now."
form_b_questions.feedback: Excellent! When we talk about 'the committee' as one unit (not individual members), we use a singular verb. The correct sentence is "The committee is deciding now."

form_b_questions.question_text: English and French ___ the two official languages.
form_b_questions.feedback: That's right! When two subjects are connected with 'and', the subject becomes plural. 'English and French' = 'They'. So we use the plural verb 'are'.

form_b_questions.question_text: One of my teachers ___ from the North-West region.
form_b_questions.feedback: Perfect! The subject is 'One' (singular), not 'my teachers' (plural). The phrase 'of my teachers' is an interrupter. We must use the singular verb 'comes'.

form_b_questions.question_text: The list of items for the market ___ very long.
form_b_questions.feedback: Excellent! The subject is 'The list' (singular), not 'items' (plural). The phrase 'of items for the market' is an interrupter. The verb must agree with 'list', so we use 'is'.

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "The teacher, as well as the students, are tired."
form_b_questions.feedback: You found it! The main subject is 'The teacher' (singular). The phrase 'as well as the students' is extra information. The verb must agree with 'The teacher', so we use 'is', not 'are'.
